extracted.intended_audience: government officials, contractors, and lawyers applying or interpreting the Eight-Hour Law (act of Aug. 1, 1892)
extracted.subtask_description: Interpretive guidance and limits on the application of the federal Eight-Hour Act (Aug. 1, 1892) to government contracts, employees, subcontractors, and specific classes of work; explains exemptions, emergencies, territorial reach, enforcement, and factual tests. Intended to determine when the statute constrains hours and who is a 'laborer or mechanic.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Government control/place_of_work
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contract is given for repairs to a Government vessel, the repairs to be made at a Government dock or under conditions which continue the vessel in the active control of the Government authorities, the eight-hour law may perhaps apply, but when ... the vessel is turned over to a contractor for repairs, at the contractor's plant ... the restrictions ... do not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test focuses on whether the work is being performed while the vessel (or work) is 'in the active control of the Government.' Examples: repairs at a government dock may fall within the act; repairs at a contractor's plant, out of government control, do not. (C.20169, Feb. 27, 1907; Feb. 9, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute self-acting / contractor responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: It was not essential that the requirement of the act of August 1, 1892, be embodied in a contract, the law itself being self-acting. The responsibility rests on contractors to comply with it, irrespective of the terms and conditions of their contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contract terms do not relieve contractors of statutory duties; contractors are directly responsible even if officers contracting on behalf of the U.S. did not include the requirement. (P.55, 311, Sept. 7, 1892; multiple opinions cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive departments cannot conclusively determine applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: It was not the duty or province of the War Department to determine such questions, but that the same were for the courts to decide, on trials, under the second section of the act...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Departments cannot lay down rules or constructions of the law that will effectively protect contractors from prosecution; applicability questions are for courts. (P.57, 36, Dec. 13, 1892; C.18811, Nov. 4, 1905.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Worker classification: seamen vs laborers/mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: While the ordinary status of certain men was that of seamen and as such not within the application of the act ... while actually engaged in 'labor upon public work' ... the men came within the application of the law. Later (Ellis v. U.S.) persons employed in dredging and rock excavation were held not to be employed 'upon any of the public works' and are to be regarded as seamen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification depends on status and the specific activity performed; some activities (e.g., snag removal) may bring seamen within the act, while other dredging/rock excavation may be treated as seamen per Ellis. Must examine factual role and controlling case law. (C.20169 decisions; Ellis v. U.S., 206 U.S. 246.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Function-based exceptions (loading vs seaman status)
rubrics_metrics.description: While persons employed on dredges and scows ... are not ... laborers or mechanics (because they are seamen), laborers employed simply to load vessels or barges are not seamen within the meaning of the foregoing premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if work occurs aboard vessels, the specific task (e.g., stevedoring/loading) can make workers 'laborers' subject to the act. (C.20169, Sept. 23, 1909; June 14, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Floating plant work and continuity of employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Where stone or other material is delivered on a breakwater from a floating plant, the work of placing, bedding, or arranging the stone ... does not come under the provision ... if the persons employed on the floating plant do the work; however, if one person is continuously employed in such work ... he should be regarded ... as engaged as a laborer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Location (floating plant) plus continuity of the individual's employment determine applicability; intermittent tasks by vessel crew may be exempt while continuous on-site employment is covered. (C.20169, Apr. 26, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary emergency standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'extraordinary emergency' ... cannot properly be construed in advance as referring or applicable to any particular class of cases. The question whether there is or was such emergency should be left to be determined by the facts of each special instance ... Merely economical considerations will not bring a case within the exception ... there must be some sudden unexpected happening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception permitting extended hours is narrow: fact-specific, time-created emergencies only (e.g., statutory appropriation deadline). Economic inconvenience or foreseeable increased expense is insufficient. (P.55, Sept. 7, 1892; C.20169, July 25, 1908; G.20169, Oct. 8, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary cannot suspend or predefine emergencies
rubrics_metrics.description: No provision is contained in the act ... for the suspension of its operation, and the Secretary of War has no power to suspend it ... Nor can he lay down in advance any general rule as to what would be such an emergency ... The question of the existence of an emergency is to be determined, in the first instance, by the person carrying on, or in charge of, the work; and, in the second, by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative advance rulings or blanket suspensions are unauthorized; the officer in charge may make an initial factual determination but is subject to judicial review. (C.16104; C.20169, Oct. 22, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption of foremen, timekeepers, inspectors, high-grade employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Foremen and timekeepers on duty with gangs of workmen employed by contractors ... cannot properly be held to come within the terms 'laborers and mechanics' ... a man whose employment is of a high grade, whose work is not manual in any sense, but ... mental labor and skill only, is not a laborer; nor can he be deemed a mechanic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titles and duties determine coverage: supervisory, managerial, or primarily mental/skilled inspector roles are excluded. Salary level, educational examination requirements, and lack of manual duty support exclusion. (C.20169, Dec. 13, 1907; Aug. 17, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Control/authority over employees required for statute to apply
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a subcontractor purchased window blinds, sashes, etc., for a public building at a factory in which the employees were working more than eight hours a day, but over whom he had no control, it was held that the statute did not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicability depends on whether the contractor/subcontractor 'employs, directs or controls' the laborers or mechanics; absence of control (manufacturing by independent supplier) typically defeats application. (C.7323, Nov. 21, 1899; C.20189, May 18, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Title/ownership of materials affects 'public work' determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether laborers or mechanics are employed on 'public works' depends largely on the question of the title to the articles or materials upon which they are at work. If the latter belong to the contractor the laborer or mechanic cannot be regarded as employed upon public works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If materials remain contractor-owned or are manufactured as contractor's property, the labor may not be 'upon public works.' Government inspection does not by itself convert the work into public work. (C.20169, July 25, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: On-site assembly vs shop manufacture distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Where lock gates were delivered in sections by a contractor, and erected in place, the act ... applied to the work of assembling the sections at the lock site and to the erection of the gates ... per contra, the construction and assembling of a lock gate in the shops of a contractor ... did not come under the act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assembly or erection at the public work site is treated as public work; off-site shop manufacture generally is not. Location of final assembly/erection is critical. (C.20169, Apr. 26, 1910; C.20169, June 21, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Installation by private company where property remains private
rubrics_metrics.description: The installation of electric lamps, conduits, etc., by a private company in the public parks ... and on the highway bridge, the lamps, etc., to remain the property of the company, held not to be a 'public work'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If installed items remain the private company's property, the activity is not a 'public work' under the statute. (C.20169, July 26, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Unloading/assorting/piling of supplies at government premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Where materials or supplies ... are delivered by a contractor on land or in a warehouse owned or leased by the United States, the work involved in unloading, assorting, and piling such materials or supplies should not be regarded as being upon a 'public work' ... if they shall have been purchased by the United States or by a contractor ... as supplies and materials to be put into the actual work of construction, such materials being delivered by the independent contractor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staged supply handling at government property does not automatically trigger the act if materials are delivered as supplies by an independent contractor and not yet part of the physical public work. (C.20169, Apr. 26, 1910.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary/offsite quarrying and preparatory work
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contractor quarried stone on the shore in the vicinity of the site of a proposed dam which he was under contract to construct for the Government, held that neither the act of August 1, 1892, nor the Army Regulations were applicable to the preliminary work of quarrying stone along the shore in the immediate vicinity of the dam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary or preparatory activities performed off the actual public work site may be outside the act; factual inquiry distinguishes preliminary quarrying from on-site construction. (C.20169, July 27, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Off-site construction that later becomes part of public work
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contractor built, on private ground, a crib, to be later floated into position and sunk as the base of a pierhead ... the labor on the crib must be considered to be on a 'public work' within the meaning of the act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If off-site work is specifically fabricated for and integrally intended to become part of public work (and not merely supplies), the labor may be treated as public work and covered by the act. (C.20169, June 11, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate-hours rule across employments
rubrics_metrics.description: The law ... is not violated, as to the hours of work of employees, so long as the aggregate of their several periods of duty does not exceed eight hours in a calendar day. ... it would be an evasion of the law to employ them for less than eight hours on the work of dam construction, and then put them on quarrying work in such manner that the aggregate of the two work periods would exceed eight hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers cannot evade the eight-hour limit by splitting duties across different gov't works or periods; total work time in the calendar day is the controlling measure. (C.20169, Jan. 9, 1908; July 27, 1909; Dec. 26, 1907.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Voting-time and paid time-off limits
rubrics_metrics.description: An executive officer cannot ... legally direct that laborers, workmen, and mechanics employed by and on behalf of the Government shall be given time without loss of pay to vote on election day, if such indulgence would reduce the number of working hours below eight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directing paid time that reduces required working hours below statutory eight per day is impermissible; however, aggregate-period counting governs overall compliance. (C.2692, Oct. 20, 1896; C.20169 opinions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of covered occupational titles (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Held that a 'hostler' at an arsenal is neither a 'laborer' nor a 'mechanic' within the meaning of the eight-hour act. Janitor for Shiloh National Park Commission ... held not to be a laborer. Stevedores and longshoremen come within the application of the act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court decisions identify specific occupations as covered or excluded—use duties, manual character, and statutory/contextual analysis rather than title alone. (C.3673; C.20169; multiple dates.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial and statutory exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of August 1, 1892, is applicable to laborers and mechanics employed on the public work of the United States in the Philippine Islands. The act was held not to apply to laborers and mechanics employed by the Board of Road Commissioners for Alaska. The act shall not apply to alien laborers employed in the construction of the Isthmian Canal within the Canal Zone (Panama) (acts of Feb. 27, 1906 and June 30, 1906).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicability can vary by territory and subsequent Congressional acts; check statutory exceptions and local enabling acts. (C.19702, May 12, 1906; C.20169, May 27, 1907; statutory acts cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement, remedies, and prosecutorial route
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not the duty of the Secretary of War to institute proceedings for violations of the act of 1892. Parties who think the law is being violated by contractors should submit their complaints to the proper United States attorney. ... the act of August 1, 1892, is penal in its nature and gives a claimant no cause of action to recover for work in excess of eight hours a day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relief is through criminal/penal enforcement (prosecution), not a civil private cause of action for overwork; administrative imposition of procurement conditions is beyond Secretary's authority. Complaints belong to U.S. Attorneys. (C.7323; C.16104; C.20169 dates cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential order coverage and Secretary exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the order of the President of September 11, 1907, directing that all persons employed as watchmen, lock tenders, lock employees, etc., shall be 'considered as covered by the eight-hour law, and that exceptions only be made by the Secretary himself on the case being reported to him,' held that exceptions were only intended to be made in cases of emergency or where, owing to the nature of the duties ... he should not be regarded as a laborer or a mechanic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain classes were presumptively covered by a Presidential order, but the Secretary may grant limited case-by-case exceptions only for true emergencies or duty nature reasons. (Presidential order Sept. 11, 1907; par. 742, A.R. 1910; C.20169, May 23, 1908.)
